Customer to provision staging VPC and add Redwood CIDR allowlist by 2027-04-18
Redwood SE to run initial smoke benchmark (50 concurrent reqs) once creds are in place
Security to accept SOC2/ISO packet and schedule short Q&A week of 2027-04-19
action_items: Maya Patel — Send network diagram + sample ALLOW list — due 2027-04-15
Leah Summers — Confirm egress policy & open ports for staging (443, 10250) — due 2027-04-18
Ravi Menon — Provide sample inference payloads and 99th percentile latency SLOs — due 2027-04-16
Karen Lowe — Share KMS/HSM requirements and existing key rotation cadence — due 2027-04-20

meeting_header: Date: 2027-04-12 | Time: 15:00 PDT | Duration: 55m | Attendees: Maya Patel (Redwood AE), Ethan Liu (Redwood SE), Daniel Park, Leah Summers, Ravi Menon, Karen Lowe, Jia Chen
summary: Weekly POC sync focused on access gating and environment blueprint. Customer is close to providing staging VPC; remaining blockers are firewall rules, KMS details, and workload payloads for benchmarking. Redwood to deliver network diagram and run initial smoke tests once credentials and allowlist are in place. Security will review compliance docs and schedule follow-up Q&A.
topics: Benchmarking plan: smoke tests and 99th pctl targets
Fallbacks: hosted vs dedicated during pilot
transcript:
[00:00] Maya: okay everyone, thanks for joining, um we'll do a 55 minute-ish checkin, quick status and then deep-dive on the network blueprint. is that good?
[00:22] Daniel: yep that works for me. can we start with what you need from infra to get staging up?
[00:32] Ethan: sure, I'll go through the minimal access set. so, for the staging VPC we need an allowlist of Redwood's egress CIDRs, access to the service endpoint over TLS 443, and optional node-level kube metrics if you want our agent to run.
[00:50] Leah: when you say agent, is that inside our cluster? what about outbound egress restrictions — our policy is deny-by-default and we need ports and hostnames.
[01:05] Ethan: yes inside the cluster, it's a light weight sidecar for telemetry; if that's a problem we can run it as an external bastion. for ports, 443 outbound to api.redwood-inference.com and 52210 for kv cache signaling, though 52210 can be tunneled over 443 if needed. (uhm) sorry sometimes the port number is different in other configs, but we'll include both in the diagram.
[01:32] Karen: 52210 rings a bell — our security team flags non-standard ports. can you provide hostnames and cert fingerprint expectations?
[01:45] Maya: absolutely, I'll put a diagram with hostname lists, FQDNs, and the expected cert chains. we'll also include an option for a VPC peering flow if Brightwell prefers private connectivity.
[02:05] Ravi: quick question on data flow — does any PII transit to Redwood's control plane in hosted mode? we're in healthcare, so data residency and minimum surface area are key.
[02:20] Maya: good point. in hosted mode, request payloads hit the Redwood control plane for routing and billing; we can redact or strip PHI before sending upstream if you want. for the pilot, we recommended using Dedicated or Private if you need zero egress of PHI.
[02:40] Daniel: can you remind us the tradeoffs? we want minimal ops overhead but strong isolation.
[02:50] Ethan: hosted is fastest to start — low friction, but less isolation. Dedicated gives you reserved GPU pools under our tenancy with isolation and SLA; Private (VPC/on-prem) is full control: you run the runtime in your environment and we provide the control plane optionally. Private requires more ops work and sync for telemetry, but is the right path for regulated workloads.
[03:18] Leah: for the POC, we were thinking staging in our cloud but isolated — so Dedicated in our VPC or Private? we need to see what's fastest.
[03:28] Maya: practically many customers start hosted for early feature validation, then move to Dedicated for the pilot. given you need data controls, I think Dedicated or Private will be a better long-term match. for this pilot, we can do Dedicated with strict allowlist and KMS integration.
[03:47] Jia: schedule wise, we're aiming to have staging smoke tests the week of 4/19. is that feasible?
[03:55] Ethan: yes, once we have VPC allowlist, service account creds, and sample payloads. total time to first smoke test ~48-72 hours typically.
[04:10] Ravi: sample payloads — what token sizes are you expecting? our production traffic is small requests but with long context sometimes.
[04:22] Ethan: send a representative set — average tokens, max tokens, concurrency targets. for benchmarks we'll run tail-latency tests: 95th and 99th percentiles for the model family you plan to use.
[04:38] Maya: I'll add a template for the payload samples in the follow-up.
[04:45] Karen: KMS — we use a cloud KMS with HSM-backed keys. how does Redwood integrate — do you require import of keys or can you call our KMS?
[04:58] Ethan: we support both. we recommend customer-managed keys (bring-your-own) where our service has a KMS encrypt-decrypt policy, or you can host keys entirely and use envelope encryption. there are a few knobs for rotation cadence and audit logs.
[05:15] Karen: audit logs are essential — we need to see token-level access logs for compliance.
[05:22] Maya: Redwood Console offers per-request tracing and token-level cost/latency breakdown — we can enable enhanced retention for the pilot. we'll include an exportable audit log in the SOC2 bundle.
[05:40] Daniel: ok, can you also outline fallback plans in case latency isn't meeting SLAs?
[05:48] Ethan: yes, automatic fallbacks are built-in. policy routing can shift to a cheaper model variant or a lower-latency shard. for the pilot we'll set conservative batch sizes and enable prefix caching to reduce token compute.
[06:05] Leah: prefix caching — does that require changes to our app?
[06:11] Ethan: minimal. it's transparent for most APIs but we ask for stable prompt templates to maximize cache hits. we'll share best-practices in the runbook.
[06:25] Jia: action items? we need a clear checklist to tick off.
[06:30] Maya: yes, I'll summarize in the follow-up — network diagram, allowlist, creds, payload samples, and security packet.
[06:40] [00:06:40] Daniel: (mumbles) also, how will billing work during Dedicated pilot — is it metered or fixed?
[06:50] Maya: Dedicated is typically reserved capacity with a monthly commit for predictability. for pilot we can do a short-term commit or a timeboxed usage plan; I'll send pricing options.
[07:05] [00:07:05] Karen: anything else on compliance? is there an on-site audit requirement?
[07:12] Maya: not for the pilot; we provide SOC2 and ISO artifacts. if you need penetration testing, we can coordinate a scoped test.
[07:24] Ethan: switching gears, quick infra checklist: kube service account with limited permissions, NodePort disabled, allowlist of outbound hosts, and a secrets bucket that Redwood can read when using staging creds.
[07:41] Leah: about secrets bucket — we cannot give read to external services; can we use signed URLs?
[07:47] Ethan: yes signed URLs or mTLS are both supported. we'll note both alternatives.
[07:56] [00:07:56] Ravi: one more technical thing — KV cache invalidation patterns. our workload has many unique prompts; will caching help?
[08:09] Ethan: caching helps when you have repeated prefixes or system prompts. for very high cardinality prompts, you still get batching benefits but cache hit rate will be lower. we can show you cache-hit projections given a sample of your traffic.
[08:25] Maya: can we tee some anonymized sample logs to Redwood for that analysis?
[08:30] Ravi: yes we can produce anonymized traces. I'll add that to the action items.
[08:37] [00:08:37] Daniel: let's talk test plan — what does success look like for the smoke test?
[08:45] Ethan: successful smoke: endpoints respond with correct structured output under nominal load, 95th < 250ms and 99th < 400ms for the chosen model, and no errors >0.1% for the sample workload. those thresholds are flexible — tell us your targets.
[09:05] Daniel: 99th under 500ms is acceptable for us initially.
[09:12] Maya: noted. we'll aim for that.
[09:16] [00:09:16] Jia: timeline recap — Maya to send artifacts by 4/15, Brightwell to open allowlist by 4/18, smoke test week of 4/19. is everyone aligned?
[09:28] Karen: yes aligned.
[09:30] Leah: we also need the SOC2 package before 4/19 — can you send that earlier?
[09:36] Maya: yes we'll attach the compliance bundle with the network package.
[09:40] [00:09:40] Ethan: quick note on bench methodology — we'll run synthetic load against a pinned model version, record latency histograms, and replay your sample payloads for quality checks. we'll also measure cost per 1k tokens.
[09:58] Ravi: when you say pinned model, can we request quantized versions? cost matters.
[10:05] Ethan: yes, we can test quantized variants; we typically recommend 4-bit quantization for cost reductions with small quality delta, but we'll surface quality regressions during the eval.
[10:20] Maya: ok, do we have any blockers preventing the allowlist from being opened? Leah?
[10:26] Leah: only internal change window scheduling — we need to sync with ops, but the allowlist itself is straightforward.
[10:34] Daniel: one operational ask — can Redwood provide a short runbook for incident playbook and rollback?
[10:42] Maya: yes, we have a one-pager incident runbook and fallback playbook for model rollback; we'll include that in the runbook pack.
[10:52] [00:10:52] Jia: any concerns about throughput? our expected concurrency is spiky — hundreds of short requests.
[11:00] Ethan: Redwood runtime supports continuous batching which smooths spikes. we'll size the Dedicated pool for concurrency targets and suggest autoscaling thresholds.
[11:12] Ravi: are there limits on token generation rates per second across the pool?
[11:18] Ethan: limits are configurable per-customer; for the pilot we'll keep conservative quotas and adjust after results.
[11:26] [00:11:26] Karen: security item — we need to know data retention defaults and how to purge logs.
[11:34] Maya: default telemetry retention is 30 days; we can configure shorter retention and purge on request. audit logs can be forwarded into your SIEM.
[11:45] Leah: forwarding to our SIEM is preferred.
[11:48] Ethan: supported via S3 export or direct syslog, whichever you prefer.
[11:54] [00:11:54] Daniel: ok this is all helpful. anything else on the blueprint?
[12:00] Maya: I'll share a network diagram and two deployment options: Dedicated-in-VPC and Private runtime. also sample IAM policies for the service account.
[12:12] Ravi: for the Private runtime, what is the expected footprint? GPUs?
[12:18] Ethan: for your model class we'd recommend 1-2 A100-equivalent nodes for small pilot or a multi-node setup for scale; we'll give exact sizing after we see token rates.
[12:31] [00:12:31] Jia: question from procurement — will there be an initial trial invoice or is this credit-backed?
[12:38] Maya: we can offer a short trial credit against the pilot; I'll connect procurement with our pricing lead.
[12:46] Karen: final security questions — can we do a brief architecture review with your security lead?
[12:53] Maya: yes, let's schedule a 30 minute session; propose Tue 4/20 or Wed 4/21.
[12:59] Leah: Wed 4/21 works for us.
[13:04] [00:13:04] Daniel: any other open items?
[13:08] Ethan: I want to flag the KV cache port again — we'll provide an option to tunnel it if security insists.
[13:16] Maya: ok, wrapping up — I'll compile the follow-up with all artifacts and action items.
[13:22] Daniel: thanks Maya, Ethan. appreciate the clarity.
[13:26] Maya: thanks everyone, we'll follow up by EOD 4/15.
[54:15] [END]
